title: Cabbage white butterfly: identification and control
subtitle: Identifying large and small white caterpillars and stopping the damage
excerpt: Cabbage white butterflies lay eggs on brassica plants from May to September, producing caterpillars that can strip a plant bare in days. The only reliable prevention is butterfly-proof netting. Identifying and removing eggs before they hatch prevents the worst damage.
sourceNotes: RHS cabbage white butterfly guide (rhs.org.uk). Garden Organic pest management resources, public domain. USDA cooperative extension notes on Lepidoptera pest management, public domain.

glossaryTerms.definition: Two distinct UK butterfly species, both of which lay eggs on brassica plants. The large white (Pieris brassicae) lays clusters of yellow eggs on the leaf underside; larvae are yellow and black and feed in groups. The small white (Pieris rapae) lays single pale eggs; larvae are plain green and harder to spot, often boring into the heart of the plant. Both species have two to three generations per year between May and September.

content.text: butterflies are the most damaging brassica pests in UK gardens. Their caterpillars feed on cabbage, kale, broccoli, Brussels sprouts, calabrese, swede, turnip, and rocket. A single large white caterpillar cluster can reduce a kale plant to a skeleton in four to five days.

Fine insect-proof mesh (maximum 1.3 mm mesh size) fitted over hoops or a rigid frame from planting to harvest is the only reliable prevention. Butterfly netting (larger mesh) excludes the adults but allows smaller insects through; insect mesh excludes both. Ensure the edges are pinned securely to the ground; butterflies will find any gap. Net before the first caterpillar is seen; once there are eggs, the damage begins within a week.

If plants are unnetted, check the underside of every leaf every three to five days from May onwards. Large white eggs are in clusters of 30 to 50 bright yellow eggs, easy to spot and crush. Small white eggs are single, pale, and harder to find; look on leaf midribs. Remove and destroy egg clusters; the leaves do not need to be removed. Checking takes a few minutes per plant and is worth doing consistently.

Hand-pick large white caterpillars, which feed on the outer leaves in visible clusters. Small white caterpillars bore into the plant hearts and are harder to remove; they leave frass (dark green pellets) as evidence. Bacillus thuringiensis (Bt) is a biological caterpillar control available as a spray; it is specific to caterpillars and harmless to other organisms. Apply when caterpillars are small for best results.

Cabbage white pupae overwinter in shed walls, fences, and garden crevices. Crush any you spot in autumn and winter to reduce next year's population. Plant fennel, dill, or cow parsley at the plot edge; their flowers attract the parasitic wasps that prey on the butterfly eggs. Clear all brassica debris after harvest so it cannot shelter overwintering pupae.
